entities.name: The Persianate Chronicle Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary: The Persianate Chronicle Corpus encompasses the vast body of historical, literary, and court literature composed in Persian across a civilizational zone stretching from Anatolia to Bengal (c. 900–1800 CE). Its crown jewel is Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (Book of Kings, c. 1010 CE) — the longest poem ever written by a single author (over 50,000 couplets), narrating Iran's mythological and historical past from creation to the Arab conquest. The corpus includes dynastic histories, court chronicles (Tarikh-i Bayhaqi, Jami' al-tawarikh of Rashid al-Din), autobiographical narratives (Baburnama of the Mughal founder Babur), and administrative manuals (Siyasatnama of Nizam al-Mulk). Persian was the lingua franca of court, diplomacy, and high culture across the Islamic East for nearly a millennium, and this literary tradition profoundly shaped the cultural identities of Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Pakistan, India, Turkey, and Central Asia.
